title: "Brushless motors"
---

Background for [Module 2](/sessions/02-motor.qmd). Not needed at the bench ---
useful for your report, and for understanding why the motor behaves the way it
does when you push it in [Module 4](/sessions/04-control.qmd).

## Start with the brushed DC motor

Every result you need for a brushless motor is easier to see in a brushed one
first, because the two obey the same electrical physics. The difference is
*how* the windings get switched, not what the machine does once they are.

A DC motor is described by two constants and one resistance. Spinning the rotor
induces a back-EMF proportional to speed, and passing current through the
windings produces torque proportional to current:

$$U_\text{emf} = \frac{\omega}{k_V} \qquad\qquad \tau = k_T \, I$$ {#eq-two-constants}

These are the same $k_V$ and $k_T$ derived in
[Module 2](/sessions/02-motor.qmd) --- inverses of each other, not independent
choices. The supply voltage splits between the back-EMF and the ohmic drop
across the winding resistance $R$:

$$U = \frac{\omega}{k_V} + R \, I$$ {#eq-voltage-balance}

Substitute $I = \tau / k_T$ and rearrange for torque, and the whole behaviour
of the motor falls out as a **straight line**:

$$\tau = k_T \frac{U}{R} - \frac{k_T}{k_V R}\,\omega$$ {#eq-torque-speed}

### Reading the torque--speed line

That line is the motor's entire steady-state character, and it is fixed by the
applied voltage. Two points define it:

- **Stall torque** $\tau_\text{stall} = k_T U / R$, at $\omega = 0$. The rotor
  is held still, there is no back-EMF, and the only thing limiting current is
  the winding resistance. This is the largest torque the motor can produce and
  also the fastest way to destroy it --- see [Thermal limits](#thermal-limits).
- **No-load speed** $\omega_0 = k_V U$, at $\tau = 0$. The rotor spins fast
  enough that the back-EMF nearly cancels the supply, so almost no current
  flows.

Everything the motor can do at that voltage lies on the line between them.
Mechanical power is $P = \tau \omega$, the product of a falling line and a
rising one, so it is a parabola peaking at **half the no-load speed** with half
the stall torque. Efficiency peaks somewhere else entirely --- much closer to
$\omega_0$, because the copper loss that dominates at low speed scales with
$I^2$ while the useful output only scales with $I$.

::: {.callout-note}
## The useful consequence

Raising the voltage shifts the line outwards without changing its slope: more
speed *and* more torque, same trade-off between them. That is why speed control
is voltage control, and why a "faster" motor at fixed voltage is a lower-torque
one.
:::

## What changes with a brushless motor

In a brushed motor the commutator and brushes are a mechanical switch riding on
the rotor: they physically reconnect the windings as it turns, so the current
always flows in whichever coil is best placed to produce torque. It works
without any electronics at all, and it wears out, arcs, and limits how fast the
motor can safely spin.

A **BLDC** motor deletes that switch. The permanent magnets go on the rotor,
the windings stay on the stator in three phases, and an external controller
decides which phases to energise based on where the rotor currently is. The
motor becomes inseparable from its driver --- this is why
[Module 3](/sessions/03-esc.qmd) exists, and why the rotor position measurement
matters so much.

What this does **not** change is @eq-torque-speed. The torque and speed
constants have the same meaning, the line has the same shape, and you size the
motor the same way. What changes is that the line is no longer the whole story:

| | Brushed | Brushless |
|---|---|---|
| Commutation | Mechanical, self-acting | Electronic, needs rotor position |
| Torque--speed line | The real limit | The *ideal* limit, then clipped by the driver |
| Wear | Brushes are consumable | Bearings only |
| Speed ceiling | Brush arcing and bounce | Commutation rate and sensor lag |
| Torque ripple | Smoothed by many commutator segments | Depends on drive scheme (trapezoidal vs FOC) |

### The envelope, not the line

The straight line assumes the supply can deliver whatever current the equations
ask for. It cannot. At stall, @eq-voltage-balance gives $I = U/R$, and with the
sub-ohm winding resistance of a small outrunner that is a number in the
hundreds of amps --- far beyond both the ESC and the motor itself.

So the driver enforces a **current limit**, and because $\tau = k_T I$ that is
directly a torque limit. The usable region becomes:

- a **constant-torque region** at low speed, flat at whatever current limit you
  set, because the ESC is holding current rather than letting the line dictate
  it;
- a **corner speed** where the back-EMF has risen enough that the supply can no
  longer push that current;
- above it, the original @eq-torque-speed line, falling to $\omega_0$.

The flat part is not physics, it is a decision. On our robot it is the decision
that keeps the motor alive at the low speeds used for swimming, where the
torque--speed line alone would happily draw enough current to cook the
windings.

## Thermal limits {#thermal-limits}

Nothing in @eq-torque-speed knows about heat, which is why the equations
cheerfully predict operating points that will destroy the motor in seconds.

Almost all the loss you care about is **copper loss** in the windings:

$$P_\text{copper} = I^2 R$$ {#eq-copper-loss}

The square is what makes this the binding constraint. Doubling the torque
doubles the current and **quadruples** the heating. A motor comfortable at
its rated current will not survive twice that for long, even though the torque
equation says it is only a factor of two.

Three practical consequences:

1. **Stall is the worst case, not the best.** At $\omega = 0$ there is maximum
   current and no rotation, so no airflow and no useful output --- all the
   input power becomes heat in the windings. A motor held at stall can burn out
   without the shaft moving at all.
2. **Continuous and peak ratings are different numbers.** A peak rating assumes
   seconds; a continuous rating assumes thermal equilibrium. Flapping is a
   *reciprocating* load, so the current is far from constant --- what matters
   for heating is the **RMS** current over the cycle, not the peak you see on
   the bench supply.
3. **Iron losses grow with speed.** Hysteresis and eddy-current losses in the
   stator scale with electrical frequency, so at the 1700 rad/s discussed in
   [Module 4](/sessions/04-control.qmd) the copper is no longer the only thing
   getting warm.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Heat is cumulative and invisible

Current is the only symptom you can see, and it appears instantly, while the
temperature it causes lags behind by tens of seconds. A run that looks fine on
the ammeter can still be depositing heat faster than the motor sheds it. When
tuning in [Module 4](/sessions/04-control.qmd), stop and touch the motor.
:::

::: {.callout-important}

## Why an outrunner

Brushless motors come in two arrangements. An **inrunner** spins a magnet rotor
inside a stationary stator, the familiar shape from a drill. An **outrunner**
inverts it: the stator sits still in the middle and the magnets are carried on
a bell that rotates around the outside. Ours is an outrunner --- it is the bell
you machine and press the shaft into in
[Module 2](/sessions/02-motor.qmd).

The reason is torque. Torque is force times radius, and in an outrunner the
magnets sit at the *largest* radius the motor's diameter allows, rather than
the smallest:

$$\tau = F \times r$$ {#eq-torque-radius}

The same tangential force from the same windings acts on a longer lever arm. It
also leaves room for more magnet poles around the circumference. Together these
raise $k_T$ for a motor of the same mass, which by @eq-two-constants means a
**lower KV** --- more torque per amp, less speed per volt.

That is the right trade for us. The wings need torque at low speed, through a
gearbox that is already multiplying by 23.04:1, and the alternative is either a
larger reduction or more current for the same result. Two secondary properties
help as well:

- **Rotor inertia.** The rotating mass is at a large radius, so the bell has
  significant inertia and acts as a flywheel. Against a reciprocating flapping
  load that smooths the speed variation over a cycle. It also means the motor
  cannot change speed quickly, which is a real cost during transients.
- **Something to attach to.** The bell is a large-diameter rotating surface,
  which is what makes the shaft press-fit in
  [Module 2](/sessions/02-motor.qmd) mechanically sensible in the first place.

The costs are real: outrunners spin more slowly for a given voltage, the
exposed rotating bell is a hazard and an ingress path, and cooling is worse
because the heat-producing stator is wrapped inside the rotor rather than
mounted against the case. The last point ties directly back to
[Thermal limits](#thermal-limits) --- an outrunner's stator sheds heat mainly
through its mount, which on our robot is a 3D-printed plate.
